events.title: Microsoft Founded
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore and his 22-year-old friend, working out of a cheap room in an Albuquerque motel, formally established a partnership to develop software for microcomputers. Their first product had been a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, licensed to the kit's manufacturer. The contract paid royalties per machine sold. Within seven years they would own the personal-computer operating system industry.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1975 — Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Originally "Micro-Soft." They moved to the Seattle suburb of Bellevue in 1979 and to Redmond in 1986. Allen left the company in 1983 after being diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma; he recovered, founded other businesses, died in 2018.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: Apple II Released
events.blurb: A young Californian computer company released their second machine — and the first mass-market personal computer designed for non-hobbyists, with built-in color graphics, a working keyboard, a plastic case, and the ability to display text and graphics simultaneously. It shipped for $1,298 and found a broad market among small businesses, schools, and households. Apple's revenues grew 700 percent a year for five consecutive years.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1977 — Apple Computer. Engineered largely by Steve Wozniak. The arrival of VisiCalc two years later made it the first computer that small businesses felt they had to buy. Apple sold over 5 million Apple IIs before discontinuing the line in 1993.

events.title: Windows 95 Launch
events.blurb: A Seattle-area software company staged one of the biggest product launches in technology history — a billion-dollar worldwide marketing campaign including exclusive use of the Rolling Stones' "Start Me Up," late-night TV appearances, lighting up the Empire State Building, and midnight retail store openings with thousands queuing to buy the shrink-wrapped boxes. The product introduced the Start menu, taskbar, and long file names to mass audiences.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1995 — Microsoft Windows 95. It sold 7 million copies in the first five weeks. Jay Leno hosted the launch event. The product was legitimately a leap forward over Windows 3.1 — and a reminder that one company now effectively controlled the world's desktop computers.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Harvey Publishes De Motu Cordis
events.blurb: A 50-year-old English royal physician published a 72-page Latin treatise correctly describing, for the first time, the circulation of the blood — with the heart as a muscular pump, arteries carrying blood outward, veins returning it, and the two sides of the heart circulating distinct streams between the body and the lungs. He had been working on the theory for nearly two decades and had presented earlier versions in lectures. The medical establishment largely ignored the book for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: 1628 — William Harvey, "Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus." Harvey's practice lost patients initially as word spread of his heresy. He lived long enough to see the theory accepted; he died in 1657 at 79, still personally treating King Charles II.

events.title: Germ Theory of Fermentation Established
events.blurb: A French chemist demonstrated through carefully controlled experiments that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by specific living microorganisms rather than by spontaneous chemical processes, and that sterilising a broth and sealing it from the air could prevent spoilage indefinitely. The experiments demolished the theory of spontaneous generation and formed the empirical backbone of germ theory.
events.revealBlurb: 1859–1861 — Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiments showed that sterilized broth stayed clear indefinitely until the curved neck was broken, letting airborne microbes in. He reportedly presented one surviving flask to the Academy in 1878 saying it had shown no signs of life in fifteen years. Some of those original flasks are still intact at the Pasteur Institute.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: World Health Organization Founded
events.blurb: A charter creating a United Nations specialized agency for public health came into force after 26 of the 61 signatories had ratified. The new organization inherited the staff and mandate of two predecessor bodies — the Office International d'Hygiène Publique and the League of Nations Health Organization. Its initial priorities were tuberculosis, malaria, venereal disease, maternal and child health, and nutrition. It had $5 million and a headquarters in Geneva.
events.revealBlurb: April 7, 1948 — World Health Organization constitution came into force. April 7 is now celebrated as World Health Day. The WHO coordinated the smallpox eradication effort 1959-1980 — arguably the most successful public health campaign in history.

events.title: HIV Identified
events.blurb: A research team at a Paris institute published a paper in the journal Science describing a new retrovirus, isolated from a lymph node of a patient with lymphadenopathy, which they believed to be the cause of AIDS. A parallel American team would publish a similar finding a year later; the credit dispute between the labs lasted years and contributed to delayed public health responses. The virus had probably crossed into humans from chimpanzees in central Africa in the early 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1983 — Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier at Institut Pasteur. Robert Gallo at the US National Cancer Institute made a similar claim in 1984. The French were eventually credited as discoverers and won the 2008 Nobel. 40 million people have died of AIDS; antiretroviral therapy since 1996 has made it a manageable chronic disease.

events.title: Intel 4004 Released
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley chipmaker released the first commercial microprocessor — a single integrated circuit 3 millimetres long containing 2,300 transistors, clocking at 740 kilohertz, capable of computing roughly as fast as the 30-tonne ENIAC 25 years earlier. It had been developed as a calculator chip for a Japanese customer. Its designers convinced Intel's management to retain the design rights and market it as a general-purpose product.
events.revealBlurb: November 15, 1971 — Intel 4004. Designers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. The 4-bit chip cost $200. Intel's 1971 product-line predecessor was the 3101 memory chip; it now sells trillions of transistors per year.

events.title: First Cellular Phone Call
events.blurb: A Motorola engineer, standing on a Manhattan street with a 1.1-kilogram "brick" prototype handset to his ear, placed a phone call to his chief rival at a competing company's research lab — and made sure to inform him what he was doing. The handset's battery gave 35 minutes of talk time after 10 hours of charging. Motorola would spend another decade getting a lighter version to market.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1973 — Martin Cooper of Motorola called Joel Engel at Bell Labs. The prototype was the DynaTAC 8000x. It sold commercially in 1983 for $3,995. Cooper later said he'd been inspired by the communicator in Star Trek.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: Windows 1.0 Released
events.blurb: An American software company released a graphical shell running on top of its text-based operating system, intended to compete with the Macintosh's point-and-click interface on IBM PC-compatible machines. Reviewers found the product clunky and slow; the original windows could not overlap, only tile side by side. Most of the PC industry continued using DOS alone for several years. Six years and three major revisions later, version 3.0 finally broke through.
events.revealBlurb: November 20, 1985 — Microsoft Windows 1.0. Product manager Tandy Trower had to beg Gates to ship it; internally there had been talk of cancelling the project. Apple sued Microsoft in 1988 over interface similarities; Apple eventually lost after six years.

events.title: iPad Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a 9.7-inch tablet — something between a smartphone and a laptop — running the same operating system as its phone. The product's name had been mocked in advance for rhyming with certain feminine-hygiene products; the device itself went on to redefine a computing form factor that previous attempts by Microsoft and others had never managed to make stick. It sold 3 million units in its first 80 days.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 2010 — Apple iPad. Steve Jobs' last major product launch. "I think we have a winner here," he said at the introduction. Microsoft's Bill Gates had been pushing tablet PCs for a decade; Apple's combination of software, battery, and price finally made the form factor work.

events.title: Emmett Till Murdered
events.blurb: A 14-year-old Black boy visiting family in a rural Southern state was abducted from his great-uncle's home in the middle of the night, tortured, shot, and thrown into a river with a cotton-gin fan tied around his neck. His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of the mutilated body, published in Jet magazine, galvanized a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1955 — Money, Mississippi. His accuser, Carolyn Bryant, admitted decades later she had lied about the encounter. Her husband and his half-brother were acquitted by an all-white jury, then sold their confession to Look magazine knowing they couldn't be retried.

events.title: Freedom Riders Depart
events.blurb: Thirteen volunteers — seven Black, six white — boarded buses in Washington, D.C. bound for New Orleans to test a recent Supreme Court ruling outlawing segregated interstate travel facilities. In Alabama their bus was firebombed outside Anniston and the riders beaten bloody by a mob in Birmingham. They kept riding. Subsequent waves continued through the summer.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1961 — sponsored by CORE. A 21-year-old John Lewis was among them and had his skull fractured. Attorney General Robert Kennedy called for a "cooling-off period;" CORE leader James Farmer replied: "We've been cooling off for 100 years."

events.title: 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing
events.blurb: A dynamite bomb planted by Klansmen exploded under the stone steps of a Black church in a Southern city on a Sunday morning, minutes before the 11:00 service. Four girls preparing for choir in the basement were killed; 22 others were injured. The bombing, eighteen days after the March on Washington, hardened national public opinion and accelerated passage of civil rights legislation.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. Victims: Addie Mae Collins, 14; Carol Denise McNair, 11; Carole Robertson, 14; Cynthia Wesley, 14. The four Klansmen responsible were slowly prosecuted over four decades; the last conviction came in 2002.

events.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Assassinated
events.blurb: Stepping onto the balcony outside Room 306 of a Tennessee motel where he was staying while supporting a sanitation workers' strike, the country's most prominent civil rights leader was shot once with a high-powered rifle from across the street. He died an hour later at a nearby hospital. He was 39. Riots broke out in more than 100 American cities within hours of the news.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1968 — Lorraine Motel, Memphis. His killer, escaped convict James Earl Ray, was captured in London two months later. The night before, King had ended a speech with: "I've been to the mountaintop. I may not get there with you, but we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land."

events.title: Fair Housing Act Signed
events.blurb: One week after the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., Congress passed and the president signed legislation outlawing discrimination in the sale, rental, and financing of housing. The bill had been stalled for two years; King's death and the rioting that followed pushed it through. It closed the third major gap in civil rights law, after employment (1964) and voting (1965).
events.revealBlurb: April 11, 1968 — Lyndon Johnson. Informally called the Civil Rights Act of 1968. Enforcement remained toothless for decades; the Department of Housing and Urban Development did not gain meaningful investigation powers until the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988.

events.title: Justinian's Code Issued
events.blurb: A Byzantine emperor's commission of ten jurists, working for 14 months, compiled nearly a thousand years of Roman legal rulings into a single four-part code. It became the foundation of civil-law systems across continental Europe and, centuries later, Latin America. Imperial-era laws contradicted themselves; the code resolved the contradictions by fiat.
events.revealBlurb: April 7, 529 — Emperor Justinian I issued the first edition. The final compilation, called the Corpus Juris Civilis, influenced the Napoleonic Code and every legal system modeled on it. Law students still read excerpts today.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Sack of Constantinople
events.blurb: A Crusader army that had set out to conquer Egypt, diverted by debts to a Venetian fleet and a pretender to the Byzantine throne, instead besieged the walls of the greatest Christian city in the world. They breached them, sacked the capital for three days, melted down ancient bronze statuary, and installed a Latin emperor. The Byzantine state never fully recovered.
events.revealBlurb: April 12-15, 1204 — the Fourth Crusade. The Venetians hauled the four bronze horses of the Hippodrome back to mount them above the entrance to St. Mark's Basilica, where reproductions stand today. Pope Innocent III was horrified and excommunicated the army — retroactively.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: Joan of Arc Burned at the Stake
events.blurb: A 19-year-old French woman, captured by Burgundian allies of the English and sold to the English crown for 10,000 livres, was tried for heresy by a church court and burned to death in a market square of a Norman city. Her executioners dug through the embers to prove she had died rather than escaped. Her remains were thrown into the Seine. She was canonized by the Vatican 489 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1431 — Rouen. A retrial in 1456 cleared her of all charges. The principal heresy she had refused to recant was wearing men's clothes. She became a Catholic saint in 1920 — six years after French troops carried her image into the trenches of World War I.

events.title: First Modern Olympics
events.blurb: The first modern Summer Olympic Games opened in an Athens marble stadium built on the foundations of a Panathenaic-festival venue 1,500 years earlier. 241 athletes from 14 nations competed in 43 events over nine days. An amateur Greek water-carrier named Spiridon Louis won the marathon, run along the road from the town to the stadium, and became an instant national hero. A 27-year-old French baron had championed the revival for nearly a decade before the games.
events.revealBlurb: April 6, 1896 — the baron was Pierre de Coubertin. Louis won his race in 2:58:50 carrying a bouquet from his village; his prize included a year's worth of free meals and a plot of land. There were no women athletes; Coubertin considered female participation "impractical, uninteresting, and incorrect."

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: Wilt Chamberlain's 100-Point Game
events.blurb: A 25-year-old 7-foot-1 Philadelphia Warriors center scored 100 points in a regular-season NBA game — 36 field goals, 28 free throws, a record that has never been approached since. The game, played at a neutral-site arena in a central Pennsylvania city, drew only 4,124 spectators; no television footage survives, and only one photograph of the 100-point moment exists. The center himself had scored 50 on a different occasion just weeks earlier; a 100-point game almost seemed inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1962 — Wilt Chamberlain, Philadelphia vs. New York Knicks at Hershey, PA. Final score: Warriors 169, Knicks 147. The iconic photo shows Chamberlain holding a piece of paper reading "100" in the locker room. His career scoring average of 30.1 points per game remains second only to Michael Jordan.

events.title: Hank Aaron Breaks Ruth's Record
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Atlanta outfielder hit his 715th career home run off a Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher, breaking Babe Ruth's 39-year-old career record in front of a sellout home crowd. He had endured a year of death threats, racist mail, and FBI protection as he approached the record. As he rounded second base, two white college students ran onto the field alongside him — security later decided they had meant only to escort him. He tipped his cap as he crossed home plate.
events.revealBlurb: April 8, 1974 — Hank Aaron at Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium, off Al Downing. His final career total was 755 home runs, which stood as the record until Barry Bonds passed it in 2007. The FBI had warned him that multiple credible plots to assassinate him were active that season.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Machiavelli Writes The Prince
events.blurb: An unemployed former Florentine civil servant, exiled from the city after a change of regime, wrote a compact political treatise in the form of advice to a hereditary ruler on how to acquire and maintain power. Its flat, unsentimental analysis of the uses of cruelty, deception, and popular love versus fear shocked readers and made its author's name a by-word for cynical politics. It remained unpublished until five years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: 1513 — Niccolò Machiavelli. The treatise was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, who almost certainly never read it. Published 1532 and promptly placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Still in print 500 years later.

events.title: Les Misérables Published
events.blurb: A 60-year-old French novelist living in exile on the Channel Island of Guernsey published a 1,500-page five-volume novel tracing the arc of a paroled convict redeeming himself over decades, set against the 1832 June Rebellion in Paris. He had been working on it, off and on, for seventeen years. The publisher sent the first volume simultaneously to seven European capitals; the author paid for advertising out of his own pocket. It was an instant international sensation.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1862 — Victor Hugo. The famous shortest correspondence in literary history happened around this book: Hugo, on holiday, wired his publisher "?" — the reply came back "!" — confirming strong sales.

events.title: Ulysses Published
events.blurb: An English-language bookshop owner in Paris published a 730-page Irish novel by a 40-year-old expatriate author that had been serialized, banned, confiscated, and partially burned in the United States. The book followed a single day — June 16, 1904 — in the lives of two Dublin men, using stream-of-consciousness narration that shifted style dozens of times across its 18 chapters. The American mail service seized copies until 1934.
events.revealBlurb: February 2, 1922 — James Joyce, 40th birthday; published by Sylvia Beach at Shakespeare and Company, Paris. The setting day — known as "Bloomsday" — is celebrated by Joyceans every June 16 with readings, pub crawls, and costumed reenactments.

events.title: The Great Gatsby Published
events.blurb: A 28-year-old American novelist published his third novel — a 218-page story about a wealthy bootlegger's obsessive love for an old flame now married to a brutish Yale football star, narrated by a Midwestern newcomer to Long Island. Reviews were respectable; sales were tepid. The author died 15 years later considering himself a failure. The book was rediscovered during WWII when Armed Services Editions shipped 155,000 copies to U.S. soldiers; it is now read in every American high school.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1925 — F. Scott Fitzgerald. Original print run: 20,870 copies. Fitzgerald earned $200 in royalties from his fourth novel "Tender Is the Night." His high-schooler daughter Scottie, who detested "The Great Gatsby," left her father's papers to Princeton.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Bombay Talkies Founded
events.blurb: A studio established in Malad, Bombay, by a London-trained filmmaker and his aristocratic actress-wife drew European technical talent — German cameramen, British equipment — to build India's first modern film facility with synchronised sound stages and a Western-style star system. It launched the careers of Dilip Kumar, Ashok Kumar, and Madhubala within its first fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1934 — founded by Himanshu Rai and Devika Rani. Rai died in 1940 while the studio was mid-production; Devika Rani, then 32, took sole control and ran it for another nine years. The studio was where a young Dilip Kumar walked in looking for work and was handed a contract he barely understood.

events.title: Awaara Released
events.blurb: A Raj Kapoor crime drama about a judge's illegitimate son — playing on the 1940s debate over heredity versus environment — became India's highest-grossing domestic release of the year and then, when dubbed and released abroad three years later, drew 64 million viewers in the Soviet Union alone, a record for any foreign film in that market. Its theme song became a street-singing anthem across Eurasia.
events.revealBlurb: December 14, 1951 — Raj Kapoor directed and starred. The song "Awaara Hoon" was so popular in the USSR, Turkey, and China that Soviet children grew up singing it phonetically in Hindi. Kapoor was reportedly stopped in Moscow streets for autographs.

events.title: Guide Released
events.blurb: A tourist guide who becomes first the manager and then the lover of a classical dancer, before his imprisonment transforms him into a reluctant holy man, gave Dev Anand his most demanding role and Waheeda Rehman her finest screen hour. Shot simultaneously in Hindi and English for two different markets, only the Hindi version became a classic; the English cut disappeared quietly.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 1965 (India) — directed by Vijay Anand, based on R.K. Narayan's 1960 Sahitya Akademi Award-winning novel The Guide. Narayan disliked the film adaptation. The English version, co-produced with a US studio, was screened briefly in America then shelved; a print was discovered decades later.

events.title: Sholay Released
events.blurb: A three-hour curry Western about two small-time criminals hired by a retired policeman to hunt a ruthless dacoit opened on India's Independence Day to a tepid first week before word-of-mouth turned it into the longest-running Indian film of all time. It played uninterrupted at a single Bombay theatre for five and a half years — 286 consecutive weeks.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1975. Director Ramesh Sippy. Amjad Khan as Gabbar Singh was nearly replaced because the scriptwriter thought his voice was too thin. The original ending showed Thakur killing Gabbar with spiked shoes — the censor board forced a reshoot. "Kitne aadmi the?" became a national catchphrase.

events.title: KGF: Chapter 2 Released
events.blurb: A Kannada-language action sequel about a gold miner's violent rise and rule over an illegal mining empire released simultaneously in five languages, broke the opening-day records of every film before it in the Hindi belt, and became the first Kannada film to gross ₹1,000 crore — a moment that announced South Indian cinema's claim on the pan-India blockbuster market.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2022 — directed by Prashanth Neel. KGF Chapter 1 had been a slow-burn cult hit two years earlier; the sequel was designed from the outset as the louder, bigger answer. Yash, who plays Rocky, was a regional star of modest fame before Chapter 1; after Chapter 2 he turned down a reported 50 offers in a single week.

events.title: Archimedes' Principle of Buoyancy
events.blurb: A Greek mathematician established that an object submerged in fluid is buoyed upward by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces — a principle explaining why objects float or sink and allowing the density of irregular objects to be measured precisely. The insight reportedly struck the mathematician while stepping into a bath, causing him to run through the streets in excitement.
events.revealBlurb: c. 250 BCE — the "Eureka" bath story was first told by the Roman writer Vitruvius about 200 years after Archimedes lived, so historians treat it sceptically. What is not disputed is that Archimedes wrote it all down carefully in On Floating Bodies, one of the oldest surviving works of physics. He also calculated an approximation of pi accurate to three decimal places.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Nuclear Fission Demonstrated
events.blurb: In a Berlin laboratory, chemists bombarded uranium with neutrons and found that the products included barium — an element roughly half the weight of uranium — proving that the atom's nucleus had split in two. The energy released per fission event dwarfed any chemical reaction by a factor of millions, a result explained by a fleeing physicist and her nephew during a walk in the Swedish snow.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1938 — Lise Meitner, who co-led the research, had fled to Sweden weeks earlier after being stripped of her position for being Jewish. Otto Hahn, who stayed in Germany, published the experimental result alone and won the Nobel Prize in 1944. Meitner received 47 Nobel nominations but was never awarded the prize.

events.title: Human Genome Project Completed
events.blurb: An international consortium announced the completion of a map of the entire 3-billion-letter chemical sequence of human DNA, covering 99 percent of gene-containing regions at 99.99 percent accuracy — two years ahead of schedule. The project, begun in 1990, required coordinating laboratories across six countries and produced a reference sequence that has underpinned virtually every major advance in genetic medicine since.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2003 — a rival private effort by Celera Genomics, led by Craig Venter, raced the public consortium and forced both teams to declare a joint "completion" in 2000. The actual finished sequence was only completed in 2003. A truly gapless human genome wasn't assembled until 2022, when long-read sequencing technology filled the remaining 8%.

events.title: First Black Hole Image Captured
events.blurb: A global network of radio telescopes, coordinated to act as a single Earth-sized dish, produced the first direct image of a black hole's event horizon — a glowing ring of superheated gas surrounding a dark central void at the centre of a galaxy 55 million light-years away. Processing the petabytes of data required a custom algorithm developed in part by a graduate student whose contribution went initially unrecognised.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 2019 — the black hole in galaxy M87 is 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun. Katie Bouman, then a postdoc, developed much of the imaging algorithm and became briefly internet-famous when a photo of her looking at the result on a laptop went viral. The press release was coordinated across six cities in six time zones simultaneously.

events.title: Mount Tambora Eruption
events.blurb: A volcano on an Indonesian island blew its top in the most powerful eruption in recorded history, spewing 150 cubic kilometres of material into the atmosphere. The sulphate aerosols lingered in the stratosphere for years, cooling global temperatures by roughly a degree and producing crop failures, famine, and snow in June across the northern hemisphere the following year.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1815 — Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia. 1816 became "the year without a summer." Mary Shelley, trapped indoors by endless rain in Switzerland, wrote Frankenstein. J.M.W. Turner's lurid sunsets from the decade owe their color to Tambora's dust.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Eyjafjallajökull Eruption
events.blurb: A glacier-capped volcano in Iceland erupted, sending a plume of fine silicate ash into the jet stream. Authorities across Europe, uncertain about engine safety, grounded all commercial aviation for six days. Around 10 million passengers were stranded, and global airlines lost an estimated $1.7 billion. Few people died, but the event showed how fragile modern mobility had become.
events.revealBlurb: April 14-20, 2010 — Iceland. The volcano's name became a running joke for newscasters. Stranded travelers included heads of state on their way to a funeral in Poland; many drove for days to get home. Rental car companies had their biggest week ever.

events.title: Typhoon Haiyan
events.blurb: One of the strongest tropical cyclones ever recorded at landfall — with sustained winds of 315 km/h — struck the central Philippines, obliterating coastal cities. A 7-metre storm surge drove ships onto city streets; the city of Tacloban lost most of its infrastructure. At least 6,300 people died, and 4 million were displaced.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2013 — Leyte province. The Filipino lead negotiator at the UN climate talks that week gave a tearful speech and began a hunger strike until "meaningful progress" was made. His country's delegation wore black.

events.title: First Animal in Earth Orbit
events.blurb: A stray mixed-breed dog named Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, a 508 kg spacecraft with no reentry capability. Laika survived liftoff and initial orbit but died from overheating within five to seven hours when a thermal regulation system failed — a fact withheld from the public for decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1957 — Sputnik 2. The Soviets announced Laika died painlessly after several days; the truth wasn't confirmed until 2002. The spacecraft had been built in under four weeks on Khrushchev's orders to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution. Laika has since been honored with a monument in Moscow and a postage stamp in more than 70 countries.

events.title: First Human in Orbit
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet Air Force pilot rode a modified intercontinental ballistic missile into a single orbit reaching 327 km altitude, completing one lap of Earth in 108 minutes before ejecting from his capsule at 7 km and parachuting separately to a field in southern Russia. The mission was fully automated; Gagarin held an emergency manual-control key sealed in an envelope in case he needed it.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1961 — Vostok 1. Gagarin was chosen partly because he was 1.57 m tall and fit the cramped capsule. He shouted "Poyekhali!" ("Let's go!") at liftoff — the same casual phrase Russian pilots use to start any flight. The module didn't fully separate and sent him spinning at 8 Gs before a wire bundle burned through.

events.title: First American in Space
events.blurb: Alan Shepard rode a Redstone rocket on a 15-minute suborbital arc reaching 187 km altitude, becoming the first American in space — 23 days after Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight. Unlike Gagarin's automated mission, Shepard manually controlled his capsule's attitude during the flight using a hand controller, though the arc itself was ballistic and unpowered.
events.revealBlurb: May 5, 1961 — Freedom 7. Shepard had been suited up and waiting in the capsule for four hours through repeated launch delays. At one point he radioed mission control: "Why don't you fix your little problem and light this candle?" His answer came 15 minutes later. He was weightless for only 5 minutes of the flight.

events.title: Apollo 13 Oxygen Tank Rupture
events.blurb: An oxygen tank in the Apollo 13 Service Module exploded 56 hours into the mission, venting both oxygen tanks to space and forcing the crew to abandon the Command Module for the Lunar Module, which was designed to support two people for two days but kept three alive for four. The crew looped around the Moon and returned safely after improvising a CO₂ scrubber from materials aboard using instructions radioed from Earth.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1970 — Apollo 13. The tank that exploded had been accidentally dropped during ground testing 18 months earlier. Mission controllers in Houston coined "successful failure" to describe the outcome. The crew consumed so little water during the return that all three were severely dehydrated; Lovell lost 6.5 kg.

events.title: Water Confirmed on the Moon
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe detected spectral signatures consistent with water molecules during its 25-minute controlled descent to the lunar south pole, with readings from a mass spectrometer increasing steadily as the probe flew toward higher latitudes. Three instruments on the orbiting spacecraft corroborated the finding, confirming that water ice is present across the lunar surface.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 2008 — Chandrayaan-1/MIP. The probe was decorated with the Indian national flag and crashed intentionally near Shackleton Crater at 85° south — making India the fourth nation to place an object on the Moon. The water discovery reversed decades of scientific consensus that the Moon was bone dry, reshaping plans for every future lunar base concept.

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: Abraham Lincoln Assassinated
events.blurb: At approximately 10:15 pm that night — five days after Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox — actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln in the head at Ford's Theatre in Washington. Lincoln never regained consciousness and died at 7:22 the following morning; he was the first American president to be assassinated.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 1865 — Ford's Theatre, Washington, D.C. Booth coordinated simultaneous attacks on Vice President Johnson and Secretary of State Seward the same night; both failed. Lincoln's bodyguard had left his post to watch the play from a better vantage point.

events.title: Pullman Strike and Federal Injunction
events.blurb: When the Pullman Company cut wages by 25 percent without reducing rents in its company-owned town south of Chicago, nearly 4,000 workers walked out that spring; within weeks, the American Railway Union's boycott of Pullman cars had paralyzed rail traffic across 29 railroads and 27 states. President Grover Cleveland dispatched federal troops and obtained a court injunction to break the strike, establishing the federal government's willingness to use military force against organized labor.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1894 — Pullman, Illinois. Eugene Debs, the ARU leader, served six months in federal prison for defying the injunction — and read socialist literature in his cell, emerging as America's most famous socialist. The strike also created Labor Day as a federal holiday, rushed through Congress as a conciliation gesture two days before Debs was arrested.

events.title: Reagan: "Tear Down This Wall"
events.blurb: Standing 100 yards from the concrete barrier dividing East and West Berlin that afternoon, President Ronald Reagan delivered a speech at the Brandenburg Gate in which he directly challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" His own State Department and National Security Council had urged him to remove the line as counterproductively provocative; Reagan insisted on keeping it.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1987 — Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin. At the time, the speech received relatively little media coverage and was dismissed as Cold War posturing by Soviet state media. Two years, four months, and 27 days later, the wall fell.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Luther at the Diet of Worms
events.blurb: A 37-year-old German theologian, summoned to a Rhineland imperial assembly under a guarantee of safe conduct, was asked to recant his written attacks on papal authority. He asked for a day to consider; the next day he returned and refused unless shown his error from scripture. The emperor placed him under imperial ban the following month. He would have been executed if the elector of Saxony had not hidden him in a castle, where he translated the New Testament into German.
events.revealBlurb: April 17-18, 1521 — Martin Luther before Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. The famous line "Here I stand; I can do no other" may be apocryphal; it appeared only in a printed account issued after the events. Luther lived another 25 years, marrying, fathering six children, and publishing prolifically.

events.title: Henry VIII Breaks with Rome
events.blurb: An English parliament passed an Act of Supremacy declaring the king — who had wanted for years to annul his marriage to a Spanish princess who had given him no male heir, and whom the pope had refused — the "Supreme Head" of the Church of England. The break with Rome was not primarily theological; the king remained Catholic in doctrine for the rest of his life. It rewrote England's religious, political, and property landscape for the next century.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1534 — Henry VIII. He had already married Anne Boleyn (his second wife) in secret in January 1533. The archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, had annulled his first marriage in May. Henry would have six wives; two were beheaded, two divorced, one died in childbirth.

events.title: Edict of Nantes
events.blurb: The first Bourbon king of France, a former Protestant who had converted to Catholicism to secure his crown ("Paris is worth a Mass"), issued an edict guaranteeing Protestant Huguenots freedom of worship in specific towns, civil equality, and the right to maintain their own fortified places. The compromise ended 36 years of Wars of Religion and was the most expansive grant of religious toleration any European state had yet made. His grandson would revoke it 87 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1598 — Henry IV of France. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, triggering a Protestant exodus of perhaps 400,000 skilled workers. Henry IV himself was assassinated by a Catholic fanatic in 1610.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: Shays' Rebellion: Armed Farmers Storm Springfield Armory
events.blurb: A force of roughly 1,500 debt-ridden Massachusetts farmers led by Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield in the depths of winter, hoping to seize weapons and overthrow a state government that was seizing their farms for unpaid taxes. State militia repelled the attack with cannon fire, killing four rebels — but the uprising terrified the nation's leaders into convening the Philadelphia Convention that produced the Constitution.
events.revealBlurb: January 25, 1787 — Springfield, Massachusetts. Daniel Shays was never caught and was eventually pardoned. George Washington, alarmed by news of the rebellion at his Mount Vernon retirement, came out of retirement to preside over the Constitutional Convention it helped cause.

events.title: Confederate Attack on Fort Sumter
events.blurb: At 4:30 in the morning, Confederate artillery opened fire on the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, beginning a 34-hour bombardment that forced the Union to surrender and formally launched the deadliest war in American history. No one was killed in the bombardment itself — two Union soldiers died in a cannon accident during the surrender ceremony.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1861 — Charleston, South Carolina. The Confederacy fired over 4,000 shells at the fort; Union defenders fired roughly 1,000 back. Nobody died in combat during the entire engagement. Within four days, President Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers, and four more states seceded to join the Confederacy.

events.title: Black Sunday: The Dust Bowl's Worst Storm
events.blurb: That spring Sunday, a wall of dust estimated at 500 to 600 feet high swept across the southern Great Plains at 60 miles per hour, blotting out the sun and turning a warm afternoon into absolute darkness across Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, and Colorado. The storm — the worst of dozens of black blizzards that had devastated the region since 1930 — was the event that gave the entire catastrophe its name: reporter Robert Geiger called the region "the Dust Bowl" the next day.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 1935 — Southern Great Plains. An estimated 300,000 tons of topsoil were displaced in a single afternoon. The Dust Bowl ultimately displaced approximately 3.5 million people from the Great Plains — the largest internal migration in American history to that point.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: Apollo 11: First Humans on the Moon
events.blurb: At 10:56 pm EDT that evening, astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped off the lunar module Eagle onto the surface of the Moon and became the first human being to walk on another world, watched live by an estimated 600 million people — roughly one-fifth of humanity. Buzz Aldrin joined him 19 minutes later; the two planted an American flag, collected samples, and departed after 2 hours and 31 minutes on the surface.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Sea of Tranquility, the Moon. Armstrong's famous line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — he swears he said it; the transmission dropped the "a." Michael Collins orbited alone overhead for 21 hours while his crewmates were on the surface. President Nixon had a speechwriter prepare a statement in case they didn't make it back.

events.title: Harihara and Bukka Found the Vijayanagara Empire
events.blurb: Two brothers from a family of provincial commanders — who had previously served both the Kakatiya and the Delhi Sultanate before being captured, converted, and then reportedly re-converted to Hinduism — established a new kingdom on the south bank of the Tungabhadra river. The city they built, Vijayanagara ("City of Victory"), grew into one of the largest in the medieval world, shielding South India's temple culture from northern incursions for two and a half centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1336 CE — Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, Tungabhadra river, Karnataka. Today their capital is called Hampi — a UNESCO World Heritage Site of 1,600 monuments sprawled over 26 square kilometres of boulder-strewn landscape. Monkeys included at no extra charge.

events.title: Timur's Army Sacks Delhi
events.blurb: A Central Asian conqueror descended from the same steppes as Genghis Khan led 90,000 cavalry across the Indus, defeated the Tughluq sultan's army in a single battle, and spent weeks pillaging Delhi. Over 100,000 people were killed in the first days; the city smelled of corpses for months afterward. The artisans Timur took back to Samarkand included the craftsmen who would build the great monuments of his capital.
events.revealBlurb: December 1398 CE — Timur (Tamerlane), Delhi Sultanate. He departed having captured so many skilled craftsmen that Delhi was depopulated. Coin minting stopped, trade collapsed, and famine followed. The Sultanate technically survived but never recovered its former power — opening the door for Babur 128 years later.

events.title: Guru Nanak Is Born
events.blurb: A child was born to a Khatri family in a Punjab village that is now in Pakistan. At age 30, he reportedly vanished into a river for three days; when he emerged, he proclaimed "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim" and began wandering across Asia — from Sri Lanka to Tibet to Baghdad — singing hymns about the oneness of the formless divine, the equality of all people, and the corruption of caste and ritual. He walked an estimated 28,000 kilometres in his lifetime.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1469 — Guru Nanak Dev Ji, born at Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan). His birthday is celebrated as Gurpurab on the full moon of Kartik. Nanak composed 974 hymns, which form the core of the Guru Granth Sahib — the living, eternal Guru of the Sikh faith.

events.title: Babur Wins the First Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Timurid prince from Fergana, having failed to hold Samarkand three times, led a force of 12,000 men and 15 cannons against the Delhi Sultanate's 70,000-strong army and 1,000 war elephants on a flat plain north of Delhi. Using a Central Asian tactic called the tulughma — flanking arcs of cavalry combined with cannon fire — he routed and killed the last Lodi sultan in a single afternoon, ending one dynasty and beginning another.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 1526 — Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire. His cannons were among the first used on an Indian battlefield. The elephants, terrified by the sound, turned and trampled their own side. Babur wrote about it all in his memoirs, the Baburnama, with the eye of a poet.

events.title: Akbar Secures the Mughal Throne
events.blurb: A 13-year-old Mughal prince was crowned emperor at Kalanaur, Punjab, moments after his father fell down a library staircase in Delhi. His regent Bairam Khan immediately faced a formidable rival — the Hindu general Hemu, who had taken Delhi with 30,000 cavalry and 1,500 war elephants. At the second Battle of Panipat, Hemu was felled by a stray arrow mid-battle, his army collapsed, and the boy king's empire was saved.
events.revealBlurb: February 1556 CE — Akbar the Great. The same king who would later abolish the jizya tax, marry Rajput princesses, invent a syncretic religion, and reportedly have three thousand women in his harem started his reign as a frightened teenager hiding behind his general.

events.title: Dunkirk Evacuation
events.blurb: Over nine days, 338,000 soldiers trapped against the sea by encircling armoured forces were lifted off a French beach by an improvised armada of naval destroyers, ferries, fishing boats, and private pleasure craft — while a rearguard held a tightening perimeter and aircraft fought overhead to keep the sky contested.
events.revealBlurb: May 26 – June 4, 1940 — Operation Dynamo. Planners hoped to save 45,000 men; they got 338,226. The "little ships" — about 700 civilian vessels ranging from lifeboats to Thames paddle steamers — became a national legend. Churchill warned Parliament not to call it a victory: "Wars are not won by evacuations."

events.title: Doolittle Raid on Tokyo
events.blurb: Sixteen medium bombers took off from the pitching deck of an aircraft carrier 650 miles out at sea — far beyond the designed launch range — and struck the enemy's capital and four other cities in daylight, causing minimal physical damage but shattering the belief that the home islands were invulnerable to aerial attack.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1942 — Lieutenant Colonel Jimmy Doolittle led 16 B-25 Mitchells off USS Hornet. None of the aircraft had enough fuel to land at friendly bases; crews ditched in China or the Soviet Union. Of 80 raiders, 3 were killed in the attacks and 8 were captured by Japan — 3 of those were executed.

events.title: Operation Torch Landings
events.blurb: American forces entered the ground war for the first time, landing simultaneously at three points along a North African coastline controlled by a French administration that had to decide within hours whether to fight the new arrivals or join them against a common enemy. The simultaneous approach from both directions trapped an entire Axis army between closing forces.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1942 — the first major American offensive operation of the war in the European theatre. French commanders initially resisted; Vichy French forces fired on US troops and sank a destroyer. A ceasefire was agreed three days later on November 11 — the 24th anniversary of the World War I Armistice.

events.title: Warsaw Ghetto Uprising
events.blurb: On the eve of a major Jewish holiday, lightly armed fighters inside an urban ghetto launched a sustained armed resistance against a force sent to complete its deportation to killing centres — holding out for nearly a month against SS troops, armoured vehicles, and systematic building-by-building destruction before the last pockets were overcome.
events.revealBlurb: April 19 – May 16, 1943. The ZOB fighters had roughly 220 pistols, several dozen rifles, and a small supply of grenades and Molotov cocktails. SS commander Jürgen Stroop demolished the Great Synagogue of Warsaw as a symbolic finale on May 16, declaring: "The Jewish quarter of Warsaw is no more." He was hanged in Warsaw in 1952.

events.title: Warsaw Uprising
events.blurb: A resistance army launched an all-out urban insurrection timed to coincide with an approaching allied army's arrival at the city's eastern bank, intending to liberate the capital before that army entered — but the expected support never came, leaving 40,000 fighters and 200,000 civilians to a 63-day battle against overwhelming force that ended in total destruction.
events.revealBlurb: August 1 – October 2, 1944. The Polish Home Army rose at 5:00 PM on August 1 with roughly 40,000 fighters. The approaching Soviet Army halted on the opposite bank and waited. Stalin also denied Allied planes permission to use Soviet airfields for supply drops for weeks. An estimated 200,000 civilians were killed; survivors were expelled and the city was systematically demolished.

events.title: Army-McCarthy Hearings
events.blurb: A televised congressional inquiry pit a grandstanding senator against the U.S. Army, which he had accused of harboring subversives. Over 36 days, 20 million Americans watched live as his bullying tactics eroded public sympathy. The defining moment came when a quiet Boston lawyer turned to him and asked, "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
events.revealBlurb: April 22 to June 17, 1954 — the lawyer was Joseph Welch. His line came on June 9, after McCarthy attacked a young associate. Six months later the Senate voted 67-22 to censure McCarthy. He drank himself to death within three years.

events.title: Warsaw Pact Founded
events.blurb: Eight communist-bloc nations signed a mutual defense treaty in the Polish capital, creating a military alliance explicitly framed as a response to West Germany's admission into the rival Atlantic alliance ten days earlier. In practice, it institutionalized Soviet command over the armed forces of its eastern European satellites.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1955 — members included the USSR, Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and Albania. It was dissolved in July 1991, six months before the USSR itself vanished. Most of its former members are now in NATO.

events.title: Hungarian Revolution
events.blurb: A student demonstration in Budapest grew within hours into a nationwide uprising against a Moscow-backed government. For twelve days, a reform-minded premier announced democratic elections and withdrawal from the eastern bloc military alliance. Then 2,500 Soviet tanks rolled into the country, crushing the revolt and killing some 2,500 Hungarians.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 to November 10, 1956 — reform premier Imre Nagy was tricked into a "negotiation," arrested, and secretly executed two years later. 200,000 Hungarians fled west. The West's failure to intervene exposed the limits of containment.

events.title: Bay of Pigs Invasion
events.blurb: A brigade of 1,400 Cuban exiles, trained and armed by the CIA, landed on a remote beach on their home island hoping to spark a popular uprising against its revolutionary government. Promised U.S. air support was withheld at the last moment. Within three days all the invaders were dead or captured. A young American president took public responsibility for the fiasco.
events.revealBlurb: April 17-20, 1961 — Kennedy, in office just three months, had inherited the plan from Eisenhower. His approval rating actually rose afterward; he quipped, "the worse I do, the more popular I get." The captured exiles were ransomed for $53 million in food and medicine.

events.title: Fall of Saigon
events.blurb: As enemy tanks crashed through the iron gates of the presidential palace in a Southeast Asian capital, U.S. helicopters lifted the last embassy staff and thousands of desperate local allies from rooftops around the city. The image of the final Huey ascending from an apartment building became the defining photograph of a failed 20-year war. Within hours, the city was renamed after a revolutionary leader who had died six years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1975 — the city became Ho Chi Minh City. The evacuation, Operation Frequent Wind, removed 7,000 people by helicopter in 19 hours. The famous "last helicopter" photo actually shows a CIA staff house, not the embassy.

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: Great Kantō Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the main Japanese island at noon, as hundreds of thousands of households were preparing lunch over charcoal braziers. The fires that erupted in the collapsed wooden city were fanned by a typhoon passing offshore, merging into a single firestorm with tornadoes of flame. Around 140,000 people died; 1.9 million were left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1923 — Tokyo and Yokohama. A persistent false rumor that ethnic Koreans were poisoning wells led to vigilante massacres of some 6,000 Korean residents. September 1 is now Japan's Disaster Prevention Day.

events.title: Exxon Valdez Oil Spill
events.blurb: An oil tanker struck a well-charted reef in an Alaskan sound after the captain left the bridge and an inexperienced third mate failed to steer back into the shipping lane. 40,000 tonnes of crude oil gushed into the pristine fjord, ultimately coating 2,100 kilometres of coastline and killing hundreds of thousands of seabirds, sea otters, and orcas.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1989 — Prince William Sound, Alaska. The captain, Joseph Hazelwood, had been drinking. It was the worst human-caused environmental disaster in US history until Deepwater Horizon in 2010. Oil is still found under beach gravel in the area today.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon Spill
events.blurb: A blowout on a semi-submersible drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico killed 11 workers and severed the riser pipe to a well 1,500 metres below the surface. Over the next 87 days, as engineers tried increasingly improbable methods to cap it, roughly 780 million litres of crude oil gushed into the sea — the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 2010 — off Louisiana. The well was finally killed in mid-September. BP paid over $65 billion in settlements, fines, and cleanup. A live-stream of the ocean-floor plume was watched by millions during the crisis; executives who claimed it was "relatively tiny" became memes.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Declared
events.blurb: The World Health Organization, having watched a novel coronavirus spread from a single city to 114 countries in ten weeks, formally upgraded its assessment from epidemic to pandemic. Within days, much of the world entered some form of lockdown — schools shut, flights grounded, stock markets crashed. Before vaccines arrived a year later, it would kill millions.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2020 — WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. The first known case had been reported in Wuhan in early December 2019. Official global death toll exceeded 7 million; excess mortality studies suggest the real number is closer to 20 million.

events.title: Heath Ledger Dies
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Australian actor was found dead in his lower Manhattan apartment by a masseuse who had come for an appointment. The cause was an accidental overdose of six prescription medications, including painkillers, anti-anxiety drugs, and sleep aids. He had recently finished filming an intense performance as the Joker in a Batman film released six months later; his family and colleagues have long disputed the "Joker-drove-him-mad" narrative that emerged. He won a posthumous Academy Award for the role.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 2008 — Heath Ledger in NYC. Daughter Matilda (with Michelle Williams) was 2. His 2008 film "The Dark Knight" was one of the first films to benefit from the surge in digital IMAX releases. His posthumous Oscar made him the second actor ever to win a competitive acting Oscar after death.

events.title: Michael Jackson Dies
events.blurb: A 50-year-old American singer widely regarded as the most successful pop star of his generation died of cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home while preparing for a 50-concert comeback tour in London. His personal physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter for administering propofol, a surgical anesthetic, to help him sleep. His death prompted an outpouring of grief that crashed major websites and sold over 35 million of his records in the following six months.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 2009 — Michael Jackson. His physician, Conrad Murray, was sentenced to 4 years and served 2. His public memorial on July 7 drew 31 million U.S. TV viewers. The "This Is It" concert film, compiled from rehearsal footage, grossed $261 million posthumously.

events.title: Ice Bucket Challenge
events.blurb: A viral social-media fundraising campaign for ALS — amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, commonly called Lou Gehrig's disease — swept the internet over the summer. Participants filmed themselves dumping a bucket of ice water on their heads, challenged friends to do the same, and donated to an ALS charity. Celebrities from Bill Gates to Donald Trump to LeBron James participated. The campaign raised $115 million for ALS research over two months and funded the discovery of a significant ALS-related gene.
events.revealBlurb: Peak: August 2014. The campaign was co-founded by Pete Frates, an ALS patient who died of the disease in 2019. The ALS Association estimated $230 million in total donations. Subsequent research identified the NEK1 gene as a contributor to ALS, directly attributable to the challenge funds.

events.title: Prince Dies
events.blurb: A 57-year-old American musician was found unresponsive in an elevator at his Paisley Park estate and recording studio outside Minneapolis, having died alone of an accidental fentanyl overdose. He had been taking painkillers for chronic hip pain aggravated by decades of acrobatic stage performances. His catalogue — 39 studio albums, countless B-sides and unreleased tracks — was so extensive that new material continued to surface from his vault for years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 2016 — Prince Rogers Nelson. He had no valid will; the distribution of his $156 million estate involved his six siblings and took six years of litigation to resolve. The tribute concerts in the weeks after his death included a Saturday Night Live special and coverage on every major music broadcast.

events.title: Notre-Dame Fire
events.blurb: A fire that began in the attic of an 850-year-old Gothic cathedral on an island in the Seine at the heart of Paris burned for nine hours, collapsing the 93-metre 19th-century spire and destroying two-thirds of the roof. Firefighters managed to save the main stone structure, the two bell towers, the three great rose windows, and most of the interior artworks. Notre-Dame's silhouette without its spire, broadcast live to the world, became a modern visual shock.
events.revealBlurb: April 15-16, 2019 — cause never conclusively determined; probably an electrical fault or a discarded cigarette. French President Emmanuel Macron pledged to reopen the cathedral within five years; it reopened December 7, 2024, more or less on schedule.

events.title: Handel's Messiah Premieres
events.blurb: A 57-year-old German-born, London-resident composer conducted the premiere of a three-hour oratorio he had written in 24 days, at a charity concert in a hall in an Irish capital. Ladies were asked not to wear hoops and gentlemen not to wear swords so more could fit in the venue. The proceeds benefited a hospital, a prison society, and a charitable infirmary. Two of the inmates were released on the night using the concert's proceeds.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1742 — George Frideric Handel at the Great Music Hall on Fishamble Street, Dublin. The "Hallelujah Chorus" became a standing-ovation custom. It's rumored King George II stood at its London premiere; no contemporary source confirms the story.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture Premieres
events.blurb: A Russian composer's commissioned patriotic overture commemorating the defeat of a Napoleonic invasion premiered at the consecration of a vast new Moscow cathedral. The score called for sixteen cannons fired in rhythm, a brass band to play "God Save the Tsar," and the bells of every church in the city ringing at the finale. The composer considered the whole thing hack-work and was embarrassed by its popularity.
events.revealBlurb: August 20, 1882 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky at the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, Moscow. The cathedral was blown up by Stalin in 1931 and rebuilt in the 1990s. American Independence Day concerts have used the cannons since a 1974 Boston Pops performance under Arthur Fiedler.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Beatles on Ed Sullivan
events.blurb: Four young British musicians from a northwestern English port city performed live on a Sunday-evening American variety show before an audience of 73 million viewers — at the time the largest in U.S. television history. The hysteria had preceded them: 7,000 people had mobbed their arrival at a New York airport two days earlier. Adult commentators dismissed them as a passing fad; younger Americans rearranged their evening to watch.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1964 — The Beatles at Studio 50, Manhattan. The crime rate during the broadcast was unusually low — even, it was said, in Times Square. They returned the next two Sundays for back-to-back appearances.

events.title: Beyoncé's Lemonade Released
events.blurb: A 34-year-old singer dropped a surprise sixth studio album, released simultaneously with a 65-minute accompanying visual film that aired on a premium cable channel. The album and film explored, over 12 tracks, themes of infidelity, race, and Black Southern heritage. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and became the only album to receive the highest score possible from Metacritic at the time. The cultural moment was so saturating that a vegetable-based cocktail name briefly came into common use.
events.revealBlurb: April 23, 2016 — Beyoncé. Film featured collaborators including Warsan Shire (poetry) and Kahlil Joseph (co-direction). The Tidal-exclusive release infuriated fans of other streaming services and drew attention to Jay-Z's struggling platform.

events.title: Founding of Rome
events.blurb: According to Roman tradition, Romulus killed his twin brother Remus in a quarrel over the city's walls, then became the first king of a settlement of seven hills beside the Tiber. Varro, working backward from consular lists, calculated the exact date centuries later and Rome adopted it as its birthday, celebrating it annually with the Parilia festival.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 753 BCE — the traditional date. Romulus allegedly populated his new city by opening it as a sanctuary for fugitives, runaway slaves, and exiles. When women were in short supply, he invited the neighbouring Sabines to a festival and had his men abduct their daughters.

events.title: Expulsion of the Last King of Rome
events.blurb: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, Rome's seventh and final king, was driven into exile after his son Sextus raped the noblewoman Lucretia, who then killed herself and thereby ignited a patrician revolt led by Lucius Junius Brutus. The Romans abolished the monarchy and replaced it with two annually elected consuls — an office designed so no single man could ever hold the power of a king again.
events.revealBlurb: September 509 BCE, traditional. Lucius Junius Brutus had spent years pretending to be an imbecile — "Brutus" literally means "dullard" in Latin — to avoid being killed by the king he was plotting to overthrow.

events.title: Publication of the Twelve Tables
events.blurb: A commission of ten patricians spent two years drafting Rome's first written legal code onto twelve bronze tablets displayed in the Forum, covering debt, inheritance, property rights, and family law. The code was a concession to plebeian demands that laws stop being secret knowledge monopolised by priestly and aristocratic insiders.
events.revealBlurb: 450 BCE, Rome. Every Roman schoolboy was required to memorise the Twelve Tables for generations afterward. One clause specified that a debtor who couldn't pay could be cut into pieces by his creditors — though historians debate whether this was ever actually carried out.

events.title: Licinian-Sextian Laws
events.blurb: After a decade of plebeian obstruction that left Rome with no consuls at all, the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus forced through three laws: one relieving debt, one limiting landholding to 500 iugera, and one requiring that at least one consul each year be a plebeian. Lucius Sextius duly became the first plebeian consul in 366 BCE.
events.revealBlurb: 367 BCE, Rome. Licinius and Sextius blocked every other piece of legislation for ten straight years to force the patricians to negotiate — essentially inventing the political hostage tactic of governmental gridlock.

events.title: The First Triumvirate
events.blurb: Julius Caesar secretly brokered a private political alliance with Rome's two most powerful men: Gnaeus Pompey, celebrated general of the East, and Marcus Crassus, the wealthiest man in Roman history. The three agreed to combine their networks and veto power to dominate legislation; the alliance had no legal standing, no name, and no public announcement.
events.revealBlurb: Late 60 BCE, Rome. Crassus, reportedly worth 200 million sesterces, once claimed no man was truly rich unless he could afford to maintain an army from his own pocket. He would later die at the Battle of Carrhae when, according to legend, the Parthians poured molten gold down his throat.

events.title: First Website Goes Live
events.blurb: The first webpage to be publicly accessible on the internet was posted from a workstation in a Swiss laboratory. It explained what the World Wide Web was, how to set up a web server, and how to use a web browser.
