Its URL ended in ".ch"; its creator had built the whole stack — browser, server, editor, protocol — in about a year and a half.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1991 — info.cern.ch, by Tim Berners-Lee. The original page was lost at one point; CERN restored a 1992 copy in 2013. The server, a NeXT workstation, is still on display with a sticker reading "DO NOT POWER DOWN — THIS IS A SERVER."

events.title: Mosaic Browser Released
events.blurb: Undergraduate students at a University of Illinois supercomputing centre released a graphical web browser for Unix, with a version for Windows and Mac released later in the year. Unlike the earlier terminal-based browsers, it could display images inline with text. Within 18 months, web traffic had grown by 10,000 percent. The browser's lead developer would leave to co-found a company that would dominate the next phase.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1993 — developed at the NCSA, lead developer Marc Andreessen. Andreessen co-founded Netscape within a year. Mosaic was free for non-commercial use, a decision that gave the web the critical mass it needed.

events.title: iTunes Store Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched an online music store selling individual songs for 99 cents each, a pricing decision its CEO had to personally negotiate with record-label executives deeply suspicious of any further internet disruption. The store sold a million downloads in its first six days. Within four years, it was the largest music retailer in the United States.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2003 — Apple. Steve Jobs had threaten to "pull the plug" on the negotiations at one point. The catalogue launched with 200,000 songs, Mac-only; Windows compatibility came in October. The per-song price model reshaped the music industry.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: Pokémon Go Released
events.blurb: A free mobile game combining augmented reality with a beloved monster-catching franchise launched initially in Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Within a week, 21 million daily active users were wandering streets and parks staring at their phones, discovering virtual creatures superimposed on physical landmarks. It became the fastest mobile game to reach $500 million in revenue and, more strikingly, got millions of sedentary users to walk outside.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Niantic Inc. Within weeks, fatal accidents, trespassing incidents, and a small bump in physical activity had all been documented. The Pokémon Go wedding, held in New York's Central Park, was among the odder cultural moments of mid-2016.

events.title: Iliad and Odyssey Composed
events.blurb: Oral-tradition epic poems about a mythic ten-year siege of a city in western Anatolia and the homecoming of a Greek king after it, composed or consolidated by a blind Ionian bard — or a school of bards working in his name — were set to writing for the first time, probably by scribes who took them down from live recitation. They would become the foundation texts of Greek literature, education, and religion.
events.revealBlurb: c. 750 BCE — traditionally ascribed to Homer. The "Homeric question" — whether one poet, many poets, or an oral tradition produced them — is still unresolved. The war they describe may reflect faint memory of Bronze Age conflicts around the archaeological site of Troy.

events.title: The Tale of Genji
events.blurb: A Japanese noblewoman serving at the imperial court of a Heian-era empress completed a 54-chapter prose narrative following the life, loves, and political career of a fictional son of an emperor. Full of psychological interiority, metaphorical poetry, and a sophisticated unreliable narrator, it is widely regarded as the world's first modern novel. It was written over more than a decade and circulated in manuscript among the court.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1010 CE — Murasaki Shikibu. The earliest surviving complete manuscript dates from the 13th century. It has been translated into English several times; Arthur Waley's 1925-33 version introduced it to the West, but recent translations are preferred for accuracy.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: First Space Station Launched
events.blurb: The Soviet Union placed the world's first space station, Salyut 1, into low Earth orbit using a Proton rocket. The 18.9-metre station provided a pressurized working volume of 90 cubic meters across three interconnected compartments and was designed to host rotating crews arriving by Soyuz capsule for extended scientific work.
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1971 — Salyut 1. The station's only successful resident crew — Soyuz 11 — spent 23 days aboard, setting a spaceflight endurance record. All three died during reentry when a faulty valve vented the cabin to vacuum; they were found in their seats, un-suited. The disaster prompted a redesign requiring all cosmonauts to wear pressure suits during docking.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Hubble Space Telescope Launch
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Discovery deployed the Hubble Space Telescope into a 612 km orbit, positioning a 2.4-meter primary mirror above Earth's atmosphere to capture ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light without atmospheric distortion. The primary mirror was later found to have been ground 2.2 micrometers too flat — a spherical aberration correctable only by a servicing mission.
events.revealBlurb: April 24, 1990 — STS-31. The mirror flaw came from a testing lens installed backward by 1.3 mm. Three years later, astronauts installed corrective optics during the first Hubble servicing mission — essentially fitting the telescope with contact lenses. Hubble has since produced more than 1.5 million observations.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Chang'e 4 Far Side Moon Landing
events.blurb: China's Chang'e 4 lander and Yutu-2 rover touched down in the Von Kármán Crater within the South Pole–Aitken Basin, the oldest and largest impact crater in the solar system, becoming the first spacecraft ever to land on the lunar far side. Because the far side never faces Earth, the mission required a dedicated relay satellite positioned at the Moon–Earth L2 point to maintain communications.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 2019 — Chang'e 4. The far side of the Moon faces away from Earth permanently due to tidal locking — no human-made object had ever touched it before. The Yutu-2 rover discovered an unusually viscous material in a small crater that scientists believe may be impact-melted basalt glass. It remains operational, the longest-running lunar rover in history.

events.title: Electron Announced
events.blurb: During a lecture at a London scientific institution, a physicist announced that cathode rays were composed of particles roughly one-thousandth the mass of a hydrogen atom — the first demonstration that atoms were not the smallest units of matter. The particles were initially called "corpuscles"; the modern name came from a suggestion by an Irish physicist the same year.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1897 — J.J. Thomson's discovery won him the Nobel Prize in 1906, and his son George Thomson won a separate Nobel in 1937 for proving the electron was a wave. Father and son together proved it was a particle and a wave — one of physics' neatest family rivalries.

events.title: Quantum Theory Proposed
events.blurb: To solve an embarrassing mathematical failure in explaining how hot objects radiate energy, a German physicist proposed a radical hypothesis: that energy is not emitted in a continuous stream but in discrete, indivisible packets whose size is proportional to frequency. He called these packets "quanta" and introduced a new constant of nature — later named Planck's constant — relating energy to frequency.
events.revealBlurb: December 14, 1900 — Max Planck later admitted he introduced the quantum as a mathematical trick he expected to discard once he found a better formula. He told his son he had just made "a discovery as important as Newton's." It took Einstein's 1905 photoelectric paper to convince physicists that quanta were real.

events.title: DNA Double Helix Published
events.blurb: A two-page letter in the journal Nature described a double-helical structure for deoxyribonucleic acid, with two chains running in opposite directions held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases. The authors noted their structure immediately suggested a mechanism by which genetic information could be copied.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1953 — Watson and Crick, aided by Rosalind Franklin's unpublished X-ray diffraction image known as "Photo 51". Their famous closing line: "It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism" — one of science's great understatements.

events.title: Plate Tectonics Theory Accepted
events.blurb: After decades of ridicule, a theory holding that Earth's crust is fractured into massive slabs drifting centimetres each year was vindicated by magnetic stripe patterns mapped on either side of mid-ocean ridges. The pattern matched predictions for seafloor spreading, explaining continental shapes, mountain ranges, and earthquake zones in a single framework.
events.revealBlurb: 1967–68 — the "plate tectonics revolution". Alfred Wegener had proposed continental drift in 1912 and been mocked for it; he died in 1930 on an expedition in Greenland. Geologists officially accepted his core idea thirty-seven years after his death.

events.title: Pulsars Discovered
events.blurb: A graduate student mapping the sky with a radio telescope noticed a repeating pulse of radio waves arriving with uncanny regularity every 1.33 seconds — far too precise to be natural noise. The signal was briefly nicknamed "LGM-1" (Little Green Men) until other examples were found across the sky, establishing a new class of rapidly rotating neutron stars more accurate than any clock then built.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 1967 — Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the anomaly in paper chart rolls she had to check by hand. Her supervisor Antony Hewish and astronomer Martin Ryle shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery; Bell Burnell was excluded despite being the one who found it, in what became one of science's most-debated Nobel omissions.

events.title: American Idol Premieres
events.blurb: A singing-competition reality show — adapted from a British format — premiered on Fox with a caustic British music executive as its lead judge, flanked by two milder American ones. The first season's audition rounds and final contestant-viewer-vote format drew enormous audiences; its first winner, a 20-year-old Texan waitress, became a genuine pop star. The show's stern British judge became a cultural shorthand for merciless critique.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 2002 — judges Simon Cowell, Paula Abdul, Randy Jackson. Host Ryan Seacrest. Season 1 winner Kelly Clarkson went on to a successful music and TV career. American Idol ran on Fox until 2016 and was revived on ABC in 2018; Clarkson's "A Moment Like This" is still its most famous product.

events.title: Lost Premieres
events.blurb: A serialized drama from ABC premiered its first episode — a 92-minute pilot for which the network had spent $14 million, then the most expensive pilot in TV history. A passenger jet crashes on a mysterious Pacific island; the survivors discover polar bears, giant submerged statues, smoke monsters, and hatches. The show pioneered the era of densely plotted serialized TV that viewers would parse online week by week, and ran for six increasingly contested seasons.
events.revealBlurb: September 22, 2004 — ABC, creators J.J. Abrams, Damon Lindelof, Jeffrey Lieber. Cast included Matthew Fox, Evangeline Lilly, Josh Holloway, and Jorge Garcia. The finale on May 23, 2010 drew 13.5 million viewers and a generation-defining debate over whether it had all made sense.

events.title: William and Kate Wedding
events.blurb: The 28-year-old second-in-line heir to the British throne married his 29-year-old university sweetheart at Westminster Abbey in London before a congregation of 1,900 and a global TV audience estimated at 2 billion. The bride wore a long-sleeved ivory lace gown; the couple kissed twice on the Buckingham Palace balcony. The marriage, closely followed by the British tabloids for years, has so far produced three children and remained notably less turbulent than the equivalent royal marriage of the generation before.
events.revealBlurb: April 29, 2011 — Prince William and Catherine Middleton. William succeeded his father Charles as Prince of Wales when Charles became king in September 2022. Their three children, in line to the throne: George (2013), Charlotte (2015), Louis (2018).

events.title: Osama bin Laden Killed
events.blurb: A team of US Navy SEALs, helicoptered into the Pakistani city of Abbottabad at night, stormed a walled compound where the founder of al-Qaeda had been hiding for over five years, 1.3 kilometres from Pakistan's premier military academy. He was killed in the raid, along with four others. His body was buried at sea from a US carrier to prevent his grave becoming a pilgrimage site. The president announced the operation in a late-night television address; crowds gathered outside the White House chanting "USA."
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2011 — Operation Neptune Spear. SEAL Team Six; President Barack Obama. Bin Laden had orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks. His death ended a 9-year, 8-month manhunt. The compound was demolished months later by the Pakistani government.

events.title: Harambe Killed
events.blurb: A 17-year-old western lowland gorilla at the Cincinnati Zoo was shot and killed by zoo staff after a 3-year-old boy climbed through a barrier and fell into the gorilla enclosure. The zoo explained that the gorilla had grabbed the child and dragged him through the water; tranquilizer darts would have taken too long. The killing triggered a wave of online outrage, internet memes, and several years' worth of "RIP Harambe" jokes that became a meta-joke of 2010s internet culture.
events.revealBlurb: May 28, 2016 — Harambe, Cincinnati Zoo. The child recovered fully. The zoo director Thane Maynard defended the decision as the only available option. The Harambe meme's peculiar staying power has been studied as a case of absurdist internet grief; election-poll write-in votes for Harambe persisted for years.

events.title: Bayeux Tapestry Completed
events.blurb: An embroidered strip of linen 70 metres long and 50 centimetres high, worked in coloured wool yarns, depicts in 58 scenes the Norman conquest of a cross-Channel kingdom — the diplomatic prelude, the invasion fleet, a victorious battle, and the death of a king by arrow. It includes 623 human figures, 202 horses, 55 dogs, and a Latin commentary running across the top.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1077 — commissioned either by Bishop Odo of Bayeux or Queen Matilda. Despite its name, it is technically embroidery, not tapestry. It survived the French Revolution only because a local lawyer hid it when a crowd tried to use it to cover an ammunition wagon.

events.title: Giotto's Arena Chapel Frescoes
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a fresco cycle covering the interior walls of a small private chapel in a northern Italian city, commissioned by a banker trying to atone for his father's usury. The artist's naturalistic figures, three-dimensional space, and emotional humanism broke decisively with Byzantine conventions and set the visual vocabulary of the next three centuries. Vasari would later date the start of the Renaissance from his work.
events.revealBlurb: 1305 — Giotto di Bondone, at the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua. Enrico Scrovegni built the chapel on the site of a Roman arena, and commissioned the frescoes to atone for the soul of his father, named in Dante's Inferno.

events.title: Leonardo da Vinci Dies
events.blurb: A 67-year-old Florentine polymath died in a small château in the Loire Valley, where the French king had invited him to retire. On the easel beside his bed was an unfinished portrait of a Florentine merchant's wife that he had carried with him for sixteen years and never delivered to the man who had commissioned it. The king would acquire the painting from his executor; the subject's name, Lisa Gherardini, would eventually become the most famous name in art.
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 1519 — Leonardo at Clos Lucé, Amboise. The portrait is the Mona Lisa, now in the Louvre, which he had begun around 1503. He bequeathed his notebooks, which he wrote in mirror script, to his assistant Francesco Melzi.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: Duchamp's Fountain
events.blurb: A French artist submitted an ordinary porcelain urinal, signed with a pseudonym and dated, as a sculpture entitled "Fountain" to the first exhibition of New York's Society of Independent Artists. The Society's board — of which he was a member — voted after heated debate to reject it. He resigned in protest. The original object was lost; the artist authorized 17 replicas over subsequent decades, each now valued at millions.
events.revealBlurb: April 1917 — Marcel Duchamp, signed "R. Mutt 1917." The original was photographed by Alfred Stieglitz and then disappeared. A 2004 survey of 500 art-world professionals named it the most influential artwork of the 20th century. An artist attacked a replica with a hammer in 2006.

events.title: Raja Harishchandra Released
events.blurb: A mythological silent film about the legendarily truthful king Harishchandra — shot in Bombay using an all-male cast because no actress would agree to appear on screen — opened at the Coronation Cinematograph in Girgaon and became India's first feature film, running 3,700 feet of hand-cranked footage. Its creator had spent over a year learning to develop film himself after being refused laboratory access.
events.revealBlurb: May 3, 1913 — Dadasaheb Phalke's debut. He was a printer by trade. Legend says he watched The Life of Christ (1906) in Bombay and decided India needed its own screen mythology. All the female roles were played by male wrestlers and cooks; no respectable woman would work in pictures.

events.title: First Filmfare Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: A British-origin film magazine inaugurated India's first popular film awards at Bombay's Metro Theatre with only five categories, winners chosen through postal ballot by readers, and a chief guest who was the US Ambassador to India. The trophy — a black-painted female figure — later became among the most recognisable objects in the entire industry and came to be known, simply, as the Black Lady.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 1954 — then called the "Clare Awards" after a recently deceased film critic. Best Film went to Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin; Dilip Kumar won Best Actor for Daag. The ceremony's postal-ballot system meant the public, not critics, decided the winners — a populist structure the awards kept for decades.

events.title: Kaho Naa... Pyaar Hai Released
events.blurb: A double-role romantic thriller built around a completely unknown actor — son of its director — became the highest-grossing Hindi film of the year and won 92 awards across ceremonies, a figure the Guinness World Records certified as a record for any single film. The overnight stardom it generated was so total that magazine covers, television specials, and public hysteria followed within days.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 2000 — directed by Rakesh Roshan, launching his son Hrithik. The film began production before Hrithik had done a single screen test beyond his father's living room. His dancing in the title track introduced a new male movement vocabulary to Bollywood that choreographers have referenced ever since.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: Baahubali: The Conclusion Released
events.blurb: The sequel to a Telugu fantasy epic that had left an entire nation debating one question — "Kattappa ne Baahubali ko kyun mara?" — opened to the largest advance booking in Indian cinema history, sold over 10 million tickets in its first weekend, and earned ₹1,000 crore net in India faster than any film before it, definitively crossing the barrier that only Hindi cinema had previously approached.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2017 — directed by S.S. Rajamouli. The two-part production cost ₹430 crore, still the most expensive Indian film made at the time. The "why" answer to the Kattappa question — withheld for two years — turned its release into a cultural event rather than just a premiere.

events.title: Executive Order 8802
events.blurb: Facing a threatened mass march on Washington organized by a prominent Black labor leader, a U.S. president signed an executive order banning racial discrimination in the defense industry and federal government. It was the first federal action against employment discrimination since Reconstruction. The threatened march was called off; the larger March would come 22 years later.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1941 — Franklin Roosevelt, pushed by A. Philip Randolph. Randolph had assembled 100,000 marchers and refused to call it off without the order. The order created the Fair Employment Practice Committee — a template for later civil rights enforcement.

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: Bloody Sunday in Selma
events.blurb: Six hundred civil-rights marchers, demanding federal protection for Black voting rights, set out from a small Alabama city to walk 87 kilometres to the state capital. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge at the edge of town, state troopers and a sheriff's posse on horseback charged them with clubs and tear gas. Televised images of a beaten John Lewis shocked the nation into action.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1965 — Selma, Alabama. Lewis's skull was fractured. Lyndon Johnson appeared before a joint session of Congress eight days later to introduce the Voting Rights Act, closing with the movement's own anthem: "We shall overcome."

events.title: Los Angeles Riots
events.blurb: Four police officers filmed beating a Black motorist named Rodney King for 81 seconds after a traffic chase were acquitted of assault by a jury with no Black members. Within hours, six days of rioting erupted across South Central Los Angeles. 63 people died, 2,383 were injured, and $1 billion in property damage was inflicted — making it the costliest civil disturbance in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: April 29 to May 4, 1992. King himself pleaded: "Can we all get along?" The officers were subsequently retried on federal civil rights charges; two were convicted. Korean-owned small businesses in "Koreatown" were disproportionately destroyed and inadequately protected.

events.title: Barack Obama Elected President
events.blurb: A first-term U.S. senator, 47 years old and the son of a Kenyan father and Kansan mother, defeated his Republican opponent by a nine-million-vote margin to become the 44th President of the United States and the first Black person elected to the office. He carried states no Democrat had won in decades, including Indiana and North Carolina.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 2008 — defeating John McCain. Obama gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park before 200,000 people. Jesse Jackson, standing in the crowd, wept on camera. Michelle Obama became the first African-American First Lady.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
events.blurb: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the proposed Constitution, providing the three-fourths supermajority required to bring the new framework of government into effect and replace the faltering Articles of Confederation. The document created a federal republic with three separated branches of power — a design that had no exact precedent in world history.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1788 — New Hampshire. Rhode Island didn't ratify until May 1790 — over a year after the government had already begun operating. North Carolina waited until November 1789, after the First Congress had already convened.

events.title: Washington's First Inauguration
events.blurb: George Washington took the presidential oath of office on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City, becoming the first executive of the new constitutional republic and establishing by his conduct nearly every precedent of the American presidency — from the two-term norm to the cabinet system to the title "Mr. President." He was the unanimous choice of the Electoral College, the only president ever to achieve that distinction.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1789 — Federal Hall, New York City. Washington reportedly added "so help me God" to the oath, though historians dispute this. He was so anxious about the job that he wrote to a friend he felt like a culprit going to execution. He almost certainly didn't want a second term either.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Dred Scott Decision
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that Dred Scott, an enslaved man who had lived in free states and territories, had no right to sue for his freedom — and that Congress had never possessed the authority to ban slavery from the territories, thereby invalidating the Missouri Compromise. Chief Justice Roger Taney further held that Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not citizens and had "no rights which the white man was bound to respect."
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1857 — Washington, D.C. The ruling was intended to settle the slavery question definitively; instead it inflamed the North and energized the new Republican Party. Dred Scott was freed by his original owner's family two months after the decision. He died 16 months later, a free man.

events.title: Iran Hostage Crisis Begins
events.blurb: Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and seized 52 American diplomats and staff as hostages, demanding that the United States extradite the deposed Shah — who was receiving cancer treatment in New York — and return his assets. The hostages were held for 444 days, paralyzing the Carter presidency and reshaping American politics for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1979 — Tehran, Iran. The hostages were released on January 20, 1981 — literally within minutes of Ronald Reagan being inaugurated. Carter spent his last night as president awake, monitoring the negotiations.
